```{=html}
<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Appendix B <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Proofs &amp; Comments</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">B.8</span> Which covector fields are differentials? (§<a class="dg-xref" href="../fields/covector-fields.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Covector_Fields">5.2</a>)</h1></header>
<p>In Section <a class="dg-xref" href="../tangent-spaces/cotangent-space.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Cotangent_Space">4.2</a> we saw that, at a single point, every covector is a differential: for every <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}_p \in T^*_p\mathcal{M}\)</span> there is some <span class="math inline">\(f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)</span> with <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}_p = (df)_p\)</span>. It is natural to ask whether this statement survives the promotion from a point to the whole manifold:</p>
<div class="dg-center"><p><em>Given a smooth covector field <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X} \in \Gamma T^*\mathcal{M}\)</span>, is there a single scalar field <span class="math inline">\(f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)</span> such that <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X} = df\)</span> everywhere?</em></p></div>
<p>The answer is “not always”, and it depends on the scale at which the question is asked: at a single point, on a small region around each point, or on the whole manifold. We go through the three scales in turn, and see that each one brings in a new obstruction. Technical names are introduced only at the end, once the ideas behind them are clear.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
```

## `Two rules for computing differentials`{=html} {#sec-two-rules-for-computing-differentials}

```{=html}
<p>Since <span class="math inline">\((df)_p(v_{\gamma, p}) \coloneqq v_{\gamma, p}(f) = (f \circ \gamma)'(\lambda_0)\)</span>, differentials inherit the rules of ordinary derivatives. For all scalar fields <span class="math inline">\(f, g\)</span> and all <span class="math inline">\(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}\)</span>: <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
    \underbrace{d\big( f \oplus_{C^\infty} \alpha \odot g \big) = df \oplus^*_\Gamma \alpha \odot^*_\Gamma dg}_{\text{linearity}},
    \qquad\qquad
    \underbrace{d\big( f \odot_{C^\infty} g \big) = f \odot^*_\Gamma dg \oplus^*_\Gamma g \odot^*_\Gamma df}_{\text{Leibniz rule}}.
\end{align*}</span> The first follows from the linearity of the ordinary derivative, and the second, at each point <span class="math inline">\(p = \gamma(\lambda_0)\)</span>, from the product rule, <span class="math inline">\(\big( (f g) \circ \gamma \big)'(\lambda_0) = f(p) \cdot (g \circ \gamma)'(\lambda_0) + g(p) \cdot (f \circ \gamma)'(\lambda_0)\)</span>. In particular, the differential of a constant function vanishes, so constants can be moved freely in and out of <span class="math inline">\(d\)</span>. Both rules hold equally for functions defined only on an open set <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{U}\)</span>, such as the coordinate maps <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}^i\)</span> of a chart. These two rules are all we need to understand what goes on below.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
```

## `Scale 1: at a point, every covector is a differential`{=html} {#sec-scale-1-at-a-point-every-covector-is-a-differential}

```{=html}
<p>Fix a chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\)</span> around <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span>. The dual chart-induced basis consists of differentials already, those of the coordinate maps, and any covector at <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span> is a combination of them, <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}_p = \sum_i \mathtt{x}_i^p \cdot (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p\)</span>. The coefficients <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{x}_i^p\)</span> are real numbers, i.e. <em>constants</em>, so by linearity they can be moved inside the differential: <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
    \mathsf{X}_p = \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}_i^p \cdot (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p = \big( d f_p \big)_p,
    \qquad \text{with} \qquad
    f_p \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}_i^p \odot \mathscr{X}^i.
\end{align*}</span> In the chart, <span class="math inline">\(f_p\)</span> is simply the <em>linear</em> function whose slopes are the components of <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}_p\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\((f_p \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1})(\alpha) = \sum_i \mathtt{x}_i^p \alpha^i\)</span>. It is defined only on <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{U}\)</span>, but a bump function extends it to all of <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{M}\)</span> without changing its differential at <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span> (see the footnote in Section <a class="dg-xref" href="../tangent-spaces/cotangent-space.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Cotangent_Space">4.2</a>). This is why it is legitimate to think of any covector at a point as a differential.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
```

## `Scale 2: on a region, the coefficients stop being constants`{=html} {#sec-scale-2-on-a-region-the-coefficients-stop-being-constants}

```{=html}
<p>Now consider a covector field <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}\)</span>. Over a chart domain it decomposes as (Section <a class="dg-xref" href="../fields/tensor-fields-and-notation.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Tensor_Fields_and_notation">5.3</a>) <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
    \left. \mathsf{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}_i \odot^*_\Gamma d\mathscr{X}^i,
    \qquad
    \mathtt{x}_i \coloneqq \left. \mathsf{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} \left\lceil \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right\rfloor \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U}).
\end{align*}</span> At every point <span class="math inline">\(p \in \mathcal{U}\)</span>, the recipe of Scale 1 produces a function <span class="math inline">\(f_p\)</span> with <span class="math inline">\((df_p)_p = \mathsf{X}_p\)</span>, but a <em>different</em> one for each point, since the slopes <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{x}_i(p)\)</span> change from point to point. The natural attempt to glue all of them into a single function is to replace the constant slopes by the component functions, <span class="math inline">\(f \coloneqq \sum_i \mathtt{x}_i \odot_{C^\infty} \mathscr{X}^i\)</span>. But now the coefficients are no longer constants, and the Leibniz rule produces an extra term: <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
    d\Big( \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}_i \odot_{C^\infty} \mathscr{X}^i \Big)
    = \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}_i \odot^*_\Gamma d\mathscr{X}^i}_{\left. \mathsf{X} \right|_\mathcal{U}}
    \;\oplus^*_\Gamma\;
    \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^d \mathscr{X}^i \odot^*_\Gamma d\mathtt{x}_i}_{\text{extra term}}.
\end{align*}</span> The extra term comes entirely from the variation of the components across the region. This particular attempt fails, but some cleverer function might still work. To decide whether one does, we need a criterion.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>A necessary condition.</strong> If <span class="math inline">\(\left. \mathsf{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = df\)</span> for some <span class="math inline">\(f\)</span>, then its components are not arbitrary: using <span class="math inline">\(df\lceil \mathcal{X} \rfloor = \mathcal{X}\lfloor f \rceil\)</span>, <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
    \mathtt{x}_i = \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \left\lfloor f \right\rceil,
    \qquad \text{i.e.} \qquad
    \mathtt{x}_i(p) = \partial_i \left[ f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right] \big( \mathscr{X}(p) \big),
\end{align*}</span> so all of them are partial derivatives of one and the same function <span class="math inline">\(f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\)</span>. Differentiating once more, and using that mixed partial derivatives commute (Schwarz’s theorem), we obtain <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
    \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \left\lfloor \mathtt{x}_i \right\rceil
    = \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \left\lfloor \mathtt{x}_j \right\rceil
    \qquad \forall \, i, j = 1, \dots, d.
    \tag{S}
\end{align*}</span> This symmetry condition does not depend on the chart used to write it, so it is a property of <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}\)</span> itself: under a change of chart, the Leibniz rule produces extra terms containing second derivatives of the chart transition map, which are symmetric in <span class="math inline">\(i\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(j\)</span> and therefore cancel in the difference of both sides of (S).</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Example.</strong> On <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{M} = \mathbb{R}^2\)</span> with the cartesian chart <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}(p) = (a, b)\)</span>, consider the covector field with component functions <span class="math inline">\((\mathtt{x}_1, \mathtt{x}_2) = (-b, a)\)</span>, i.e. <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X} = (-\mathscr{X}^2) \odot^*_\Gamma d\mathscr{X}^1 \oplus^*_\Gamma \mathscr{X}^1 \odot^*_\Gamma d\mathscr{X}^2\)</span>. Then <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
    \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^1} \left\lfloor \mathtt{x}_2 \right\rceil = 1
    \;\neq\;
    -1 = \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^2} \left\lfloor \mathtt{x}_1 \right\rceil,
\end{align*}</span> so there is no scalar field <span class="math inline">\(f\)</span> with <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X} = df\)</span>, neither on <span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}^2\)</span> nor on any open set, however small. Pointwise, of course, nothing is wrong: at a point <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span> with <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}(p) = (a_p, b_p)\)</span>, Scale 1 gives <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}_p = (df_p)_p\)</span> with <span class="math inline">\(f_p = (-b_p) \odot \mathscr{X}^1 \oplus a_p \odot \mathscr{X}^2\)</span>. What fails is that these linear functions differ from point to point, and no single function reproduces all of them at once.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Exact fields do not form a module.</strong> The Leibniz rule also explains why the module <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma T^*\mathcal{M}\)</span> of Section <a class="dg-xref" href="../fields/covector-fields.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Covector_Fields">5.2</a> had to be built from all smooth sections, and not only from differentials. Differentials are closed under addition, <span class="math inline">\(df \oplus^*_\Gamma dg = d(f \oplus_{C^\infty} g)\)</span>, but not under s-multiplication by scalar fields: rearranging the Leibniz rule, <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
    h \odot^*_\Gamma df = d\big( h \odot_{C^\infty} f \big) \oplus^*_\Gamma (-f) \odot^*_\Gamma dh,
\end{align*}</span> which, because of the last term, is in general not a differential. For instance, <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}^1 \odot^*_\Gamma d\mathscr{X}^2\)</span> on <span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}^2\)</span> has components <span class="math inline">\((\mathtt{x}_1, \mathtt{x}_2) = (0, a)\)</span> and violates (S).</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>The condition is also sufficient on a ball.</strong> Conversely, suppose that <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}\)</span> satisfies (S) on a chart domain whose image <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U})\)</span> is a ball centred at the origin of <span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}^d\)</span>. Writing <span class="math inline">\(\bar{\mathtt{x}}_i \coloneqq \mathtt{x}_i \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\)</span> for the chart representatives of the components, we can build the missing function explicitly, by adding up the values of <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}\)</span> along the straight segment from the origin to each point <span class="math inline">\(\alpha \in \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U})\)</span>: <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
    F(\alpha) \coloneqq \int_0^1 \sum_{i=1}^d \bar{\mathtt{x}}_i(t \alpha) \, \alpha^i \, dt,
    \qquad
    f \coloneqq F \circ \mathscr{X}.
\end{align*}</span> Differentiating under the integral sign, using (S) to exchange the indices, and recognizing a total derivative in <span class="math inline">\(t\)</span>, <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
    \partial_j F(\alpha)
    &amp;= \int_0^1 \Big[ \bar{\mathtt{x}}_j(t\alpha) + \sum_{i=1}^d t \, \alpha^i \, \partial_j \bar{\mathtt{x}}_i(t\alpha) \Big] dt
    \overset{\text{(S)}}{=} \int_0^1 \Big[ \bar{\mathtt{x}}_j(t\alpha) + \sum_{i=1}^d t \, \alpha^i \, \partial_i \bar{\mathtt{x}}_j(t\alpha) \Big] dt \\
    &amp;= \int_0^1 \frac{d}{dt} \Big[ t \, \bar{\mathtt{x}}_j(t\alpha) \Big] dt
    = \bar{\mathtt{x}}_j(\alpha),
\end{align*}</span> i.e. <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{x}_j = \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \lfloor f \rceil\)</span>, and hence <span class="math inline">\(\left. \mathsf{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = df\)</span>. Since every point has a chart neighbourhood whose image is a ball, we conclude that at this scale (S) is both necessary and sufficient: <em>a covector field is a differential near every point if and only if it satisfies (S).</em></p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
```

## `Integrating a covector field along a curve`{=html} {#sec-integrating-a-covector-field-along-a-curve}

```{=html}
<p>To understand the last scale we need one more tool, which in fact we have just used: the integral <span class="math inline">\(F(\alpha)\)</span> above adds up the values of <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}\)</span> along a segment. In general, given a smooth curve <span class="math inline">\(\gamma\)</span> and a parameter interval <span class="math inline">\([\lambda_a, \lambda_b]\)</span>, at each <span class="math inline">\(\lambda\)</span> the covector <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}_{\gamma(\lambda)}\)</span> can eat the velocity of the curve, producing a real number. Adding up these numbers along the curve defines the <strong>integral of <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}\)</span> along <span class="math inline">\(\gamma\)</span></strong>, <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
    \int_\gamma \mathsf{X} \coloneqq \int_{\lambda_a}^{\lambda_b} \mathsf{X}_{\gamma(\lambda)}\big( v_{\gamma(\lambda)} \big) \, d\lambda
    = \int_{\lambda_a}^{\lambda_b} \sum_{i=1}^d \mathtt{x}_i\big(\gamma(\lambda)\big) \cdot \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) \, d\lambda,
\end{align*}</span> where the second expression holds whenever the curve stays inside the chart domain <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{U}\)</span>. If <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X} = df\)</span>, the integrand is, by definition of the differential and of the velocity, <span class="math inline">\((df)_{\gamma(\lambda)}\big( v_{\gamma(\lambda)} \big) = v_{\gamma(\lambda)}(f) = (f \circ \gamma)'(\lambda)\)</span>, and the fundamental theorem of calculus gives <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
    \int_\gamma df = f\big(\gamma(\lambda_b)\big) - f\big(\gamma(\lambda_a)\big).
\end{align*}</span> The integral of a differential only depends on the endpoints of the curve, not on the path in between. In particular, for a <em>closed</em> curve, one that returns to its starting point, the integral of a differential always vanishes.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p>This also works in the opposite direction, and tells us how to <em>build</em> <span class="math inline">\(f\)</span> from <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}\)</span> on a connected manifold. Fix a reference point <span class="math inline">\(p_0\)</span>, and define <span class="math inline">\(f(p)\)</span> as the integral of <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}\)</span> along any curve from <span class="math inline">\(p_0\)</span> to <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span><sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-1" id="fnref-1" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="Footnote 1">1</a></sup>. This is a sensible definition precisely when the result does not depend on the curve chosen; and since two curves from <span class="math inline">\(p_0\)</span> to <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span> form a closed curve when the second is run backwards, this happens precisely when the integral of <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}\)</span> along every closed curve vanishes. In that case, extending a curve from <span class="math inline">\(p_0\)</span> to <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span> by a short segment along the <span class="math inline">\(j\)</span>-th coordinate direction of a chart shows that <span class="math inline">\(\partial_j \left[ f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right] = \bar{\mathtt{x}}_j\)</span>, i.e. <span class="math inline">\(df = \mathsf{X}\)</span>. Therefore, <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
    \mathsf{X} = df \text{ for some } f \in C^\infty(\mathcal{M})
    \quad \iff \quad
    \int_\gamma \mathsf{X} = 0 \text{ for every closed curve } \gamma.
\end{align*}</span></p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
```

## `Scale 3: on the whole manifold, local primitives must glue`{=html} {#sec-scale-3-on-the-whole-manifold-local-primitives-must-glue}

```{=html}
<p>The construction on a ball worked because every point could be reached from the centre along a straight segment lying inside the region, so every closed curve in it could be shrunk continuously to a point, and (S) guarantees that the integral does not change during the shrinking, so it must vanish. On a region with a “hole”, a closed curve winding around the hole cannot be shrunk, and its integral may be non-zero even when (S) holds everywhere. In that case <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}\)</span> is a differential near every point (Scale 2), but the local functions cannot be glued into a single one.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p><strong>Example.</strong> On the punctured plane <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{M} = \mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{0\}\)</span>, with the same two charts as in Appendix <a class="dg-xref" href="../examples/example-fields.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Example_Fields">C.4</a> (the cartesian chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}(p) = (a, b)\)</span>, and the polar chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\)</span>, defined off the ray <span class="math inline">\(\{a \leq 0, \, b = 0\}\)</span>), consider the covector field with component functions <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
    \left( \mathtt{x}_1, \mathtt{x}_2 \right) = \left( \frac{-b}{a^2 + b^2}, \frac{a}{a^2 + b^2} \right).
\end{align*}</span></p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p><em>It satisfies (S) everywhere:</em>  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^1} \left\lfloor \mathtt{x}_2 \right\rceil
            = \frac{b^2 - a^2}{(a^2 + b^2)^2}
            = \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^2} \left\lfloor \mathtt{x}_1 \right\rceil.
        \end{align*}</span>  By Scale 2, it is therefore a differential near every point.</p></li>
<li><p><em>It is a differential on <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{V}\)</span>:</em> its components coincide with those of <span class="math inline">\(d\mathscr{Y}^2\)</span>, the second row of the Jacobian <span class="math inline">\(\left( \textrm{\runic ᛞ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \right)^2_{j} = \partial \mathscr{Y}^2 / \partial \mathscr{X}^j\)</span> computed in Appendix <a class="dg-xref" href="../examples/example-fields.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Example_Fields">C.4</a>. Hence <span class="math inline">\(\left. \mathsf{X} \right|_\mathcal{V} = d\mathscr{Y}^2\)</span>: on <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{V}\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}\)</span> is the differential of the polar angle <span class="math inline">\(\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(b, a)\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p><em>It is not a differential on <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{M}\)</span>:</em> along the unit circle <span class="math inline">\(\delta(\lambda) = (\cos \lambda, \sin \lambda)\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(\lambda \in [0, 2\pi]\)</span>, whose velocity has components <span class="math inline">\(\dot{\delta}^i_\mathcal{U}(\lambda) = (-\sin \lambda, \cos \lambda)\)</span>,  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \int_\delta \mathsf{X}
            = \int_0^{2\pi} \Big( (-\sin \lambda) \cdot (-\sin \lambda) + \cos \lambda \cdot \cos \lambda \Big) \, d\lambda
            = 2\pi \neq 0,
        \end{align*}</span>  although <span class="math inline">\(\delta\)</span> is a closed curve.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>The would-be function <span class="math inline">\(f\)</span> is the angle <span class="math inline">\(\theta\)</span> itself, and it fails for a simple reason. Near every point there is a local function whose differential is <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}\)</span>, namely a local determination of the angle. Following the circle, each local determination must continue the previous one, and after a full turn we come back to the starting point with <span class="math inline">\(\theta + 2\pi\)</span> instead of <span class="math inline">\(\theta\)</span>: the local functions exist, but they cannot be glued into a single-valued, smooth function on the whole punctured plane. The polar chart avoided the problem by cutting the plane along a ray, but that cut is precisely what makes it a <em>local</em> description.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
```

## `The names of things`{=html} {#sec-the-names-of-things}

```{=html}
<p>With the ideas in place, here is the standard vocabulary, which the reader will meet in the literature.</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>In the language of differential forms, covector fields are called <em>1-forms</em>.</p></li>
<li><p>A covector field of the form <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X} = df\)</span> is called <strong>exact</strong>.</p></li>
<li><p>A covector field satisfying (S) is called <strong>closed</strong>. The condition is usually written as <span class="math inline">\(d\mathsf{X} = 0\)</span>, where <span class="math inline">\(d\)</span> is the <em>exterior derivative</em>, an operation extending the differential <span class="math inline">\(f \mapsto df\)</span> from scalar fields to 1-forms. We have seen that every exact field is closed.</p></li>
<li><p>The <strong>Poincaré lemma</strong> states that on a contractible region – one that can be continuously shrunk to a point, such as a ball – every closed covector field is exact. The construction of <span class="math inline">\(F\)</span> in Scale 2 is its proof for a ball.</p></li>
<li><p>The <strong>first de Rham cohomology group</strong> <span class="math inline">\(H^1_{\text{dR}}(\mathcal{M})\)</span> collects the closed covector fields, regarding two of them as equivalent when they differ by an exact one. It is trivial precisely when every closed covector field is exact, and it measures, in this sense, the “one-dimensional holes” of <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{M}\)</span>: it is trivial for <span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}^d\)</span> or any contractible manifold, and non-trivial for the punctured plane or the circle <span class="math inline">\(S^1\)</span>.</p></li>
</ul>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p>In summary, the answer to our question depends on the scale at which it is asked, and each scale adds one requirement to the previous ones:</p>
<ol class="dg-enumerate dg-depth-1">
<li><p><em>At a point:</em> every covector is a differential, <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}_p = (df_p)_p\)</span>, because its components are constants and can be moved inside <span class="math inline">\(d\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p><em>Locally:</em> once the components become functions, the Leibniz rule gets in the way, and a covector field is a differential near every point if and only if it is closed. Closed or not, every covector field is still locally a combination of differentials with function coefficients, <span class="math inline">\(\left. \mathsf{X} \right|_\mathcal{U} = \sum_i \mathtt{x}_i \odot^*_\Gamma d\mathscr{X}^i\)</span>: what may fail is being <em>a single</em> differential.</p></li>
<li><p><em>Globally:</em> a closed covector field is a differential on all of <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{M}\)</span> if and only if its integrals along all closed curves vanish, i.e. if and only if its local primitives can be glued together. This is guaranteed when <span class="math inline">\(H^1_{\text{dR}}(\mathcal{M})\)</span> is trivial, e.g. on any contractible manifold, but even there only for closed fields: the field of the first example, on <span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}^2\)</span>, is not a differential anywhere.</p></li>
</ol>
<p>This is why, in the main text, generic covector fields are denoted by <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}, \mathsf{Y}, \dots\)</span>, and the symbol <span class="math inline">\(df\)</span> is reserved for exact ones.</p>
<section class="dg-footnotes" role="doc-endnotes"><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-1" role="doc-footnote"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-1" aria-label="Back to the text">1</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>Here curves are allowed to be piecewise smooth, since joining two curves end to end generally produces a corner; the integral is then computed piece by piece.</p></div></div></section>
```
